lawyer:
Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan with Sarder Abul Hossain, Advocates ------ For the Petitioner 
Mahbubey Alam with Md Mozammel Hossain, Advocates  ------ For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Zamini Bala Das ------ Petitioner 
Vs.
Abdul Aziz and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J : Plaintiff obtained the Rule upon making a revision application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure against judgment and decree dated 10-8-03 passed by the District Judge at Narayanganj in Title Appeal No. 09 of 03 reversing those dated 1-12-2003 passed by the Joint District Judge, Court No.2 at Narayanganj in Title Suit No.4 7 of 99 and dismissing the suit.

2. On 10-3-99 the plaintiff Zamini Bala Dasi instituted the suit against Abdul Aziz Miah, predecessor of opposite parties for a decree of declaration of title in northern 36 decimals out of 76 decimals of land of CS plot No. 274 appertaining to CS khatian No. 86 fully described in the schedule to the plaint.

3. Plaint case, in short, is that being owner in possession one Gour Hari transferred entire 76 decimals of land of said plot No. 274 to Juthisthir Das Poddar and Arjun Das Podder and delivered possession. Both Juthisthir Das Poddar and Arjun jointly lived with brother Bhim Das Poddar at the time. Said brothers acquired the land with the income of the joint family. Bhim Das Poddar died leaving a son Bhupati Bhushan Das as his only legal representative. By a family partition effected by a registered deed in 1936 Juthisthir and Arjun and their nephew Bhupati Bhusan Das partitioned their entire property and by way of that partition Juthistir got said northern 36 decimals of land in his share and Bhupati Bhusan got the rest 36 decimals. While he was thus owner in possession of said northern 36 decimals of land, Juthistir died leaving two sons Shuvangkar Das Poddar and Bankeswar Das Poddar as his only legal representatives. By another family partition between Subhankar and Bankeswar said land fell in the share of Suvangkar and Bankeswar got other land. Then Suvangkar died leaving three sons, namely, Sulaksman, Sudarshan and Sudhangsu as his only legal representatives. By a registered deed of sale being No. 6959 dated 7-11- 51 said Sulaksman, Sudarshan and Sudhangshu transferred said 36 decimals of the suit land to the plaintiff and delivered possession. SA record of rights was accordingly prepared and finally published in her name and she possessed the suit land on payment of rents. As the defendant claimed that he got title in the suit land the plaintiff was constrained to institute the suit.

4. The defendant contested the suit by filing a written statement. His main defence was that by two registered sale deeds being No. 965 and 966 dated 30-10-70 the plaintiff transferred the suit land to Golap Banu and her husband Jainal Abedin and delivered them possession. Said Golap Banu and Jaibal Abedin then transferred the suit land by sale deed being 45789 dated 6-12-79 to the defendant. The defendant got the land mutated in his name and possessed on payment of rent to the Government.

5. On the pleadings the issues were framed regarding the maintainability of the suit in the manner and form framed; transfer of the suit land by the plaintiff by sale deed No. 965 and 966 dated 30-1-70; title, possession and dispossession of the plaintiff by the defendant; and the relief the plaintiff was entitled to.

6. Both plaintiff and defendant examined five witnesses each. Documents produced by the plaintiff were marked Exhibits 1 to 6 while those of the defendants marked as Exhibit 'Ka'.

7. On the evidence oral and documentary on record, the trial Court held that the sale deeds being No. 965 and 966 dated 30-1-70, Exhibit 'Kha' were forged and created through false personification and that the defendant dispossessed the plaintiff during the course of the suit and the defendant acquired no title by purchase from said Golap Banu and Jainal Abedin. Upon such view, the trial Court decreed the suit declaring title of the plaintiff in the suit land and directed her to make an application for possession.

8. Accordingly, the plaintiff made an application for recovery of possession which was registered as Title Execution Case No. 01 of 2003. By order dated 21-1-2003 a Writ of delivery of possession was issued and same date the process server returned the process by delivery of possession to the decree holder.

9. Against the decree, the defendant presented Title Appeal No.9 of 2003 before the District Judge at Narayanganj. By the impugned judgment and decree, learned District Judge allowed the appeal, set aside the decree of the trial Court and directed the Nazir to restore possession to the defendant. Hence, the Rule.

10. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Advocate for the petitioner, submitted that the judgment was not a proper judgment of reversal as it neither set aside the findings of the trial Court nor adverted to the reasons for the findings.

11. Secondly, he submitted that when the trial Court found the deeds 965 and 966 were forged and created through false personification, learned District Judge committed serious error in dismissing the suit without reversing those findings.

12. He submitted that as the plaintiff was dispossessed in the course of the suit she was not required to amend the plaint to restoration and recovery of possession and the suit, therefore, would not fail. In support, he cited Hamida Begum vs Murad Begum, PLD (1975) SC 624.

13. Lastly, he submitted that trial Court having committed no error in restoring the possession to the plaintiff who was dispossessed in the course of the suit and the appellate Court erred in law in directing restitution without deciding the issues. He cited in support, Abdul Jalil Munshi and another vs Abu Bakar Siddique, 35 DLR (AD) 42; Badal Kanti Das vs Abul Hashem and ors, 47 DLR (AD) 6 and Md Abdul Nasir and ors vs People's Republic of Bangladesh and another, 28 DLR 392.

14. There is no dispute that by successive devolutions, the plaintiff Zamini Bala Das ultimately acquired the suit land by purchase by sale deed No. 6959 dated 7-11-51 from Sulaksman, Sudarshan and Sudhangshu. Both SA and RS record of rights were prepared and finally published in her name. She possessed the suit land on payment of rents, accordingly.

15. Further case of the plaintiff is that while she was thus in possession of the suit land, in 1999 the defendant made claims over the suit land and threatened to dispossess her. Whereupon she was constrained to institute the suit.

16. On the other hand, the case of the defendant is that the plaintiff transferred the suit land by two registered deeds being Nos. 965 and 966 dated 30-1-70 to Golap Banu and her husband Jainal Abedin. Then, said Golap Banu and Jainal Abedin transferred the suit land to the defendant by a sale deed being No. 45789 dated 6-12-79 and delivered possession. Thus the defendant acquired the suit land, got his name mutated and possessed since then on payment of rent to the Government.

17. When the defendant admits the title and possession of the plaintiff up to 1970, the burden is on him to prove his acquisition of title and possession from her. The defendant produced sale deed Nos. 965 and 966 in original, Exhibit 'Kha'. But neither the scribe of the deeds nor the person who identified the plaintiff Zamini Bala before the sub-registrar could be produced and examined by the defendant. The defendant did not take any step to prove the execution and registration of the deeds.

18. With regard to possession, the defendant as PW 1 claimed that Golap Banu and Jainal Abedin possessed the suit land since 30-1-70. Then they transferred the suit land to him on 6-12-79 and he since then possessed.

19. In cross-examination, he said that he was not a witness to the deeds of Golap Banu and another. Execution and registration of the deeds were not done before him. He, however, denied that said deeds were obtained by false personification. He also denied that how Golap Banu and Jainal Abedin possessed the land was not stated in his written statement. He could not even say who the scribe was and who the witnesses to said deeds were. He, however, said that the land was never mutated in the names of Golap Banu and her husband nor they have paid any rent.

20. DW 2 Md Jamir Ali testified that the suit land was originally owned by a Hindu woman. He could not say how long she possessed. Earlier, IRRI paddy used to be produced in the suit land. Now, there were shops. He could not say whether Zamini Bala grew IRRI.

21. DW 3 Haji Shahidul Islam testified that he got land east and north of the suit land. The defendant possessed the suit land for last 22/23 years, first by cultivation and then making and leasing out shops for last 10/11 years.

22. In cross-examination, he said that the land was used for growing paddy and jute, Hindus used to grow. He said it was not true that the defendant did not possess the suit land before 12-4-99 or the plaintiff was dispossessed by the defendant. The defendant possessed 20/22 years, before him Hindus enjoyed whom he knew since he had land near the suit land. He could not know whether they were male or female. He did not see any Hindu female possessing. It was land of paddy and jute Hindus cultivated.

23. DW 4 Md Giusuddin deposed that there were shops on the suit land for last 10/12 years, defendant raised the shops. Defendant possessed the suit land for 20/22 years. He possessed under the defendant. He said that it was not true that the defendant dispossessed the plaintiff 8/10 years ago. He did not see any woman named Zamini Bala in the suit land. He could not say in which side the suit land was situated or the boundaries thereof. He did not know the suit land nor he could say whether Zamini Bala used to possess the suit land before 12- 4-99.

24. DW 5 Dilip Kumar testified that he was a scribe and wrote deed No. 45789 dated 6-12-79. In cross examination, he stated that he did not obtain the LTI of Golap Banu nor did he sign her name.

25. On the above evidence of the defendant the possession of Golap Banu and Jainal Abedin is not at all proved. Then, the possession of the plaintiff must be held to have continued. PW 2 to PW 4 in one voice corroborated the plaintiff's daughter PW 1 that her mother Zamini Bala Das all along possessed the suit land and was then dispossessed therefrom by the defendant.

26. Appellate Court at the outset wrongly approached the suit from a standpoint not sanctioned by law. He most erroneously placed the onus on the plaintiff to prove every fact including the fact that she did not execute and register the sale deeds, Exhibit 'Kha'. It is the general rule that the plaintiff is to prove his/her case in order to succeed and get a decree. But when title and possession of the plaintiff up to certain time is admitted by the defendant, then the onus is shifted to the defendant to prove how the plaintiff lost his/her title and possession and how he got his title and possession from the plaintiff. Appellate Court found that the suit land was recorded in both SA and RS khatians in the name of the plaintiff and she possessed on payment of rents. Yet it demanded proof from her that she did not execute and register the deeds when the definite case of the plaintiff is that she did not execute and register the deeds in question. A Court cannot demand from a party to prove a negative fact.

27. Both the Courts below are found to have dwelt upon the report of an expert dated 13-6-2000. At the instance of the plaintiff, opinion of an expert was sought for on the LTIs that appear on the deeds, Exhibit 'Kha'. The expert sent her report. The plaintiff filed an objection to such report. The suit was adjourned for examination of the expert up to 29-5-2002. When the expert did not turn up, how the appellate Court could blame the plaintiff for his/her failure in examination of the expert is not understood. And when the report could not be tested by examination and/or cross-examination of the expert it would remain in the record as a mere opinion. No Court should use such opinion in support of its any finding.

28. It appears from the record that about 60 thumb impressions of the plaintiff along with those as appear on deed Nos. 965 and 966 were sent to a hand- writing expert for his opinion as to whether questioned LTls on said deeds were of the plaintiff Zamini Bala. When the expert did not turn up, the trial Court took the responsibility upon itself and compared the questioned thumb impressions with the thumb impressions of Zamini Bala on the plaint, her deposition sheet and Vokalatnama and came to a finding that the questioned thumb impressions on the deeds did not tally with her admitted thumb impressions. In the circumstances, the course adopted by the trial Court could neither be objected to nor be said to be 'not sanctioned by law. The appellate Court did not use its sight to see as whether the trial Court was correct. But the appellate Court failed to appreciate such finding of the trial Court.

29. We have compared the thumb impressions on said deeds with the thumb impressions of plaintiff Zamini Bala on the Vokalatnama, deposition sheet and the plaint and find the difference between them so marked and striking to any naked eye that the appellate Court would have confirmed the finding of the trial Court had it so compared.

30. Result being, the deeds must be held to be brought into existence by forgery, fabrication and false personification. Existence of Golap Banu and Jainal Abedin is also not proved. The defendant, therefore, obtained no title by his deed dated 6-12- 79, Exhibit 'Ga'.

31. It was contended on behalf of the defendant-opposite-party that the suit was not maintainable in the absence of any relief for declaring the deeds being 965 and 966 dated 30-1-70 Void and/or cancellation thereof. It was also contended that the suit without amendment of the plaint" for recovery of possession on the claim of dispossession of the plaintiff on 12-4-99 from the suit land must be held to be hit by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

32. It appears from the record that on the prayer of the plaintiff by order dated 5-4-99 the trial Court directed the parties to maintain status quo in respect of possession of the suit land. On 20-4-99 the plaintiff made an application for a mandatory injunction for restoration of possession claiming that on 12-4-99 the defendant dispossessed her from the suit land. On 21-4-99 she also made an application for taking action against the defendant for violation of the order of status quo dated 5-4-99. The application was registered as Violation Miscellaneous Case No. 09 of 1999. The defendant opposed the applications by filing written objection. On the evidence, the trial Court found that the defendant dispossessed the plaintiff violating the order of status quo. The appellate Court did not at all consider such vital question of the suit.

33. It is now well settled that if a party is dispossessed from the suit land during the course of a proceedings the Court is not only entitled but also duty bound to restore such party to possession in order to ensure status quo ante. In Abdul Jalil Munshi v Abu Bakar Siddique, 35 DLR AD 42 the Appellate Division held:

"If a party to a suit does an act to bring about a change in the state of things existing at the date of the suit or just prior to that date, in order to forestall a possible order of the court, the Court may, in an appropriate case, in exercise of its inherent power, require the offending party, by issuing a temporary injunction in mandatory form, to restore the status quo ante.

It further held:

"....this principle is in consonance with fair administration of justice and this power of making an order of mandatory injunction on an interlocutory application may be exercised irrespective of the merits of the main case as it is one of the main concerns of a Court of law to see that no one dares to interfere with the course of justice by presenting the Court with a fait accompli. "

34. The Appellate Division followed the principle in Babul Kanti Das vs Abul Hashem 47 DLR (AD) 6.

35. Rule 7 of Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure requires every plaint shall state specifically, the relief the plaintiff claims either simply or in the alternative, and it shall not be necessary to ask for general or other relief which may always be given as the Court may think just to the same extent as if it had been asked for.

36. Rule 8 of Order VII rules where the plaintiff seeks relief in respect of several distinct claims or causes of action founded upon separate and distinct grounds, they shall be stated as far as may be separately and distinctly.

37. In view of above rules, the plaintiff is obliged only to seek relief clearly and distinctly or in the alternative on the causes of action at the time of institution of the suit. He is entitled to adjudication on the basis of his rights on the date of the suit. But in the course of the suit, if new causes arise, then the plaintiff may seek for further relief thereon. Sometimes, the intervention by a party in the proceeding of a suit may oblige the Court to restore the parties to status quo ante so that none of the parties takes any advantage and they are ensured to contest at the level they found each other at the commencement of the suit. Proceeding before a Court of law must be taken by the parties to be solemn and hallowed, If any party is found to be guilty of interfering with the course of the proceeding, it is not only an obligation of the affected party to seek for appropriate relief but also the duty of the Court to act decisively in order to protect and uphold the sanctity of the authority of law.

38. In Mohammad Abdul Nasir and others vs People's Republic of Bangladesh and another 28 DLR 392, a Division Bench of this Division in similar situation took the view:

"The scope of the suit is to be determined with respect to the allegations in the plaint and not with reference to the allegations of written statement. If after institution of the suit, some events take place and the plaintiff is dispossessed from a part of the suit land, the subsequent event will not affect the suit as framed.

... ... Ordinary rule is that rights of the parties must be determined as it stands at the date of action and not on the basis of the right which has occurred after institution of the suit. In an appropriate case the Court can mound its decree in order to suit the event which has taken place after institution of the suit. In such case the object of the rule is that the Court should not reject the plaint and try the case by taking notice of the subsequent event".

39. The Court was therefore, fully empowered to direct the defendant to restore possession in disposing of the miscellaneous case for violation. But the Court directed the plaintiff to make a formal application for recovery of possession. Accordingly, the plaintiff made an application for possession. The application was registered as a title execution proceeding and ultimately, possession was delivered to the plaintiff. The course adapted by the Court was not necessary. The Court could have achieved the same goal by directing the defendant to restore possession in the decree.

<u>40. We have already found that sale deed Nos. 965 and 966 dated 30-1-70 were forged and created since the plaintiff did not execute and register the documents. The documents are therefore, void ab initio. When a document is void ab initio that need not be avoided; Cf: Hamida Begum v Murad Begum, PLD 1975 SC 624.</u>

41. The deeds never affected the rights of the plaintiff. The plaintiff was therefore not required to seek any declaration either for setting aside or cancellation of them. Nor was she required to amend the plaint.

42. In Sufia Khanam vs Faizun Nesa, the Appellate Division held, inter alia.

"In view of what has been discussed above we hold that the impugned sale-deed which has been held void by the Court because of fraud need not be cancelled and that the direction for amending the plaint for the purpose of cancellation of the document is unnecessary."

43. In the facts of the case and the evidence, oral and documentary, on record, learned District Judge missed the vital issues and consequently, his decision was seriously flawed both on fact as well as in law. The impugned judgment and decree therefore, cannot be sustained, which have no doubt, resulted in failure of justice.

44. In the result, the Rule is made absolute with cost. The impugned judgment and decree are thereby set aside and those of the trial Court restored. The suit is decreed as prayed for.

Send down the record at once.

End.
